title: Playing soft solos at tables
summary: Between sets he took his horn to individual tables and developed a very soft controlled open tone that could not be heard past the table.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Whom did you play with with Curtis Moseby?
Oh, gee I can't remember half the names. I can't even hardly remember the personnel of the band. I know Marshall Royal was one. And gee, I don't remember too many of the fellows.

Another interesting thing in all of these bands at that time was we played for the dancing of the patrons on the floor. Then between sets we would play for the entertainers who went out on the floor and dispersed among the audiences, and would sing individual songs at the individual tables.

Well, this time like if we had eight pieces in the orchestra, four of us would go out this set -- four of us would go out the next set. And that was real nice because a lot of times -- after we'd been there for awhile, we would do indivi-dual soloing, which I did quite a few solos. You know -- just to individual tables -- for the people at a table.
And I developed a little gimmick which was sort of interesting. I could play so soft, open horn, that I would

hold the horn in the middle of your table and play an open melody, and you couldn't hear it past the table. You know -- sort of a -- not a sub-tone, but a soft, very soft control. Of course I lost that after I started playing with big bands you know. You couldn't control anymore that way.

But that was my forte at that time. I'd get many calls over come play me so and so. And I would play this in this sub-tonish fashion. Which wasn't a sub-tone -- the tone wasn't blocked -- it was that I could control it so evenly that you could put it right in your ear -- right up to your ear, and the melody -- you could hear the melody.
You must have been getting a following right about that time.
Yeah, I had quite a little following. Of course the money was short. But it was something that I was quite proud of -- to be able to do.
